civil-war-1918.claim_en: The Finnish Civil War was a war of liberation against a Bolshevik plan to annex Finland and replace its population with Russians, and Finland's independence was secured when Russia/the Soviet Union lost World War I.
Lenin's book The State and the Revolution, written in Helsinki, contains a direct call to political terror.
Soviet Russia's involvement in the Finnish Civil War included sending troops and declaring war on the Whites, and the article's infobox should treat Germany and Russia symmetrically.
The Whites in the Finnish Civil War were the government's troops, and Soviet Russia was not a direct belligerent in the same de jure sense as the Finnish factions.
The Civil Guard was clearly Finland's largest civic organization during its existence.
Executions and terror claimed more victims than battles in the Finnish Civil War, and both sides suffered deaths from terror.
The Finnish People's Delegation rebelled against the legitimate government, whose forces were the armed forces of the Republic of Finland.
Establishing a de jure state of war between Finland and Russia during the 1918 civil war was difficult, and Soviet Russia was not a party to the battles.
The Finnish Civil War was fought between the forces of official Finland and forces attempting a revolution.
Thousands of "class traitors" who supported right-wing Finland belonged to the Civil Guards.
The Red Guards were armed by Russian occupation forces, 10,000 to 14,000 Russians fought on the Red side, and South Ostrobothnian Civil Guards stopped them from taking Ostrobothnia.
The Reds and Russians aimed to conquer South Ostrobothnia in February 1918, but were stopped by the South Ostrobothnian Civil Guards.
The 1918 war should be seen as a war of liberation rather than a civil war because it ended with the Treaty of Tartu between Finland and Russia.
Lenin's book 'The State and Revolution' contains a direct exhortation to political terror.
The White side in the Finnish Civil War represented the legitimate Finnish government and its republican army fighting against rebels, rather than being one of two warring factions.
The Finnish Civil War was an armed coup instigated by Lenin and an overreaction by the Reds, and German intervention was not decisive for the outcome.
Russia, Sweden, and the German Empire participated as states in the Finnish Civil War.
The White forces in the Finnish Civil War were the official troops of the Republic of Finland fighting against rebels.
The 1918 election of Friedrich Karl as King of Finland was carried out by a rump parliament using the disputed 1772 constitution and never took effect in practice.
The 5,800–6,000 underage victims of the Finnish Civil War were aged 9–20, and the youngest was a nine-year-old Red Guard boy.
The youngest soldier who died in the Finnish Civil War was a nine-year-old Red Guardist.
The White side in the Finnish Civil War consisted of legitimate government troops rather than the White Guard, and Soviet Russia was not a combatant on the Red side.
Signs of the 1918 battle are still visible in Tampere.
Estonia or Estonians helped Finland during the Finnish Civil War.
White émigrés participated in the Finnish Civil War and supported the Whites by capturing Helsinki, Lahti, and other southern Finnish cities alongside the German Empire's army.
The commanders-in-chief of the Finnish Civil Guards were Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim, Wilhelm Alexander Thesleff, Karl Rudolf Walden, Georg Didrik von Essen, and Lauri Malmberg.
Lenin recognized Finnish independence not out of gratitude, but because he expected Finland to have a revolution and join the Soviet Union.
Political terror and executions were not a major cause of death compared to battles in the Finnish Civil War.
Sweden participated in the Finnish Civil War with leaders Carl August Ehrensvärd and Erik Palmstierna and 700–800 Swedish volunteers.
The Finnish Civil War broke out on the night of 26–27 January 1918, marked by a red lantern raised on the Workers' House tower in Hakaniemi, Helsinki.
The total number of victims of the White terror may remain permanently unresolved, with the Suomen sotasurmat project listing 7,370 Red victims as executed, shot, or murdered and 1,767 as missing.
Executions and prison camps claimed more victims in the Finnish Civil War than actual battles.

continuation-war.claim_en: The railway in question should be referred to as the Murmansk Railway rather than the Kirov Railway.
The Red Army stopped the Finnish offensive at Koromyslovo in Ošta, far outside both the territories ceded in the Winter War and East Karelia.
Foreign Minister Eljas Erkko caused the Winter War and the deaths of 85,000 people by rejecting and concealing a Soviet territorial proposal that Mannerheim supported.
Finland was a neutral party that wanted to negotiate and fought a separate war from Germany during the Continuation War.
Finland was Germany's ally in the Continuation War rather than fighting a separate war, as Finnish officers helped plan Operation Barbarossa and the war depended on German support.

In May 1941, Finland's highest leadership decided to participate in Germany's planned military campaign against the Soviet Union on the condition that Finland remain independent, Germany attack first, and Finland join only after Soviet hostilities began.
Hitler's speech merely conveyed the impression, rather than revealing the truth, that Finland was politically allied with Germany.
The Winter War was a military victory for the Soviet Union and a political defensive victory for Finland.
Germany viewed Finland's participation in the Continuation War as part of a larger German plan rather than a separate war, as evidenced by the marching song "Von Finnland bis zum Schwarzen Meer".
Finnish troops were and still are true guerrillas and resilient, and Finland performed well relative to its small army.
The Continuation War was a military and political victory for the Soviet Union.
The relevant Winter War figures were 330, 114, 40, and 5 instead of 250, 130, 39, and 3.
The Continuation War ended in a Soviet victory.
The Red Army did not treat wounded prisoners of war at all in accordance with international agreements and often shot them immediately.
The Winter War was a Soviet victory.
Finland had to carefully take the Soviet Union's interests into account in its foreign policy.
Foreign historiography on Finland's alliance with Germany during the Continuation War has relied on Soviet historiography.
Racism against Russians was cultivated to raise morale and served as a guarantee of Finnish success in the Winter War.
The Soviet Union broke off the Moscow negotiations and subsequently made repeated demands on the Baltic states that led to their annexation into the Soviet Union.
The Finnish offensive in 1941 halted before the German setback at the Battle of Moscow, and Finnish military deaths in 1941 exceeded those of both the Winter War and the 1944 Soviet offensive.
Finland was politically allied with Nazi Germany in its war aims and Finns lacked the courage to admit it.
Russians have subsequently tried to claim that the Winter War was merely a small border skirmish.
The figure of over 40,000 German troops in Finland at the outbreak of the Continuation War is unsourced and incorrect.
The United Kingdom and the United States were belligerents in the Continuation War with 15,000 troops fighting in the Arctic theater.

The Continuation War resulted in a Soviet Pyrrhic victory, with Finland ceding territory and paying reparations while retaining its independence, following pre-war Finnish-German military cooperation.
Kirill Meretskov was the commander instead of Kliment Voroshilov, and the associated figures were 330, 114, 40, and 5.
The Finnish offensive in 1941 was halted before the German setback at the Battle of Moscow, and Finnish military deaths in 1941 exceeded those in the Winter War and the 1944 offensive.
The pretext for the Winter War was the Terijoki Government's 1 December 1939 appeal for help to the Soviet Union rather than the Shelling of Mainila.
The Soviet Union occupied Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia in June 1940 and annexed them as Soviet republics in August 1940.
The Battle of Tali-Ihantala is the largest and bloodiest battle in the history of the Nordic countries.
The Kingdom of Italy participated in the Continuation War with 100 troops under Giuseppe Bianchini.
Mussolini and Italian Foreign Minister Ciano demanded arms shipments through Germany to Sweden and partly in secret to the Finnish front.
Finland was not occupied, and in 1948 Joseph Stalin toasted the Finnish army for being a good army.
In June 1939, the Finnish government decided to establish the army headquarters in Mikkeli for a future war, and it was established in July.
The Finnish army called the Red Army 'Ryssä' and Red Army soldiers called Finns 'Ghost soldiers' because of their white snowsuits.
Mannerheim's refusal of Hitler's proposal to encircle Leningrad allowed Soviet troops to prepare unhindered for the summer 1944 major offensive.
Italy was a belligerent in the Continuation War with 100 men under Giuseppe Bianchini.

Mannerheim's term as President of Finland ended on 11 March 1946 rather than 4 March 1946.

Mannerheim's letters to a French friend allegedly reveal that he was homosexual, and President Paasikivi ordered them sealed to protect national unity.
